name: Hip Fracture
tagline: A proximal femur fracture — usually a low-energy fall in an older adult with weak bone, where the fracture is the visible half of the problem and the frailty behind it is the other.
whatItIs: A break of the proximal femur, grouped by where it sits relative to the joint capsule: femoral neck (intracapsular), intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric (both extracapsular). That one distinction drives blood supply, fixation choice and complications.

The femoral head is fed retrograde by retinacular branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery running up the neck. An intracapsular fracture can tear them, which is why displaced neck fractures risk avascular necrosis and nonunion and are often replaced rather than fixed.

Mechanism is usually a low-energy fall from standing height onto weakened bone — a fragility fracture, and by definition osteoporosis until proven otherwise. High-energy hip fractures in the young are a different injury with different priorities.

It behaves as a sentinel event, not an isolated injury: one-year mortality runs about 15–30% depending on the series, many never regain their prior mobility or independence, and the fracture itself predicts the next one.
diagnosis: History: the fall and why it happened — mechanical trip versus syncope, arrhythmia, hypoglycemia, sepsis, or a medication. A fall with no adequate mechanism is a workup, not just a fracture.

Exam: groin or lateral hip pain, inability to bear weight, and in a displaced fracture a shortened, externally rotated leg. Pain on gentle axial load or log-roll is sensitive. Document distal pulses and sensation.
First imaging: AP pelvis plus a cross-table lateral of the affected hip. Compare the two sides — a subtle break in the trabecular pattern or a step in the femoral neck cortex is easy to miss.
A normal radiograph does not exclude it. If the patient cannot bear weight and the films look clean, get MRI (or CT if MRI is unavailable) for an occult or nondisplaced fracture.
Classify to plan surgery: Garden I–IV for femoral neck (I–II nondisplaced, III–IV displaced), and stable versus unstable for intertrochanteric patterns.
Preoperative workup is for fitness and cause, not delay: CBC, chemistry, type and screen, ECG. Also send calcium, vitamin D and TSH — the osteoporosis assessment starts now, not at discharge.

meds.drug: Regional block (fascia iliaca or femoral nerve)
meds.use: Preoperative analgesia, ideally within hours of arrival
meds.note: Better pain control with far less opioid — which is the point in a patient at high delirium risk
Scheduling it reduces total opioid dose; check the total daily dose against any combination products

meds.use: Breakthrough pain only, at reduced geriatric doses
meds.note: Undertreated pain also causes delirium — the goal is the least opioid that allows movement, not none

meds.use: VTE prophylaxis, continued 28–35 days after surgery
meds.note: Hip fracture surgery carries one of the highest VTE risks in orthopedics

meds.use: Surgical prophylaxis within 60 minutes of incision
meds.note: Redose for long cases or major blood loss

meds.use: Secondary fracture prevention, started after surgical repair
meds.note: HORIZON-RFT gave the first infusion within 90 days of repair: clinical fractures 8.6% vs 13.9%, all-cause mortality 9.6% vs 13.3%. Load vitamin D first and correct hypocalcemia

meds.use: Replete before and alongside antiresorptive therapy
meds.note: Starting a bisphosphonate into vitamin D deficiency risks symptomatic hypocalcemia

nursing: Pain control is delirium prevention. Advocate early for a regional block, give scheduled acetaminophen, and reassess after movement rather than only at rest.
Screen for delirium every shift with a validated tool. Watch for the quiet, hypoactive form — it is missed far more often than agitation and carries the worse prognosis.
Protect the skin from the moment of arrival. These patients lie still on a hard surface in the emergency department for hours; heel and sacral pressure injuries begin there, not on the ward.
Do not apply skin traction — it does not improve pain or outcomes. Position for comfort with the leg supported.
Get them up the day after surgery unless the surgeon has restricted weight bearing. Early mobilization drives fewer pneumonias, fewer clots and better function.

Do not leave them NPO all day. Follow the anesthesia team's fasting rule — clear fluids are usually allowed until two hours before surgery — and get it re-clarified every time the case slips down the list. A frail patient starved from midnight for an afternoon theatre slot arrives dehydrated and more delirious, which undoes everything else here.
Guard sleep, bowels, hydration and hearing aids and glasses. These unglamorous items are the substance of delirium prevention.
Before discharge: confirm someone owns the osteoporosis treatment and the falls assessment. Both are commonly assumed to be someone else's job and then done by nobody.
medStudent: Anchor everything on intracapsular versus extracapsular. Intracapsular threatens the femoral head's blood supply; extracapsular does not, which is why the operations differ.

The usual plan: nondisplaced neck → internal fixation; displaced neck in an older adult → arthroplasty; intertrochanteric → cephalomedullary nail or sliding hip screw. For the displaced neck, total hip rather than hemiarthroplasty if they walked independently outdoors with no more than a stick, have no comorbidity making it unsuitable, and are expected to manage daily activities independently beyond two years.
Operate early — within 24–48 hours, which AAOS rates on strong evidence. Delay beyond that tracks with more complications; the argument is about how much earlier helps, not whether waiting hurts.
Spinal and general anesthesia give similar outcomes. REGAIN found no meaningful difference in death, ambulation or delirium, so the choice is individualized rather than dogmatic.
Answer the question the fracture asks: why did they fall? Cardiac, neurologic, infectious and iatrogenic causes all present as a hip fracture in an older adult.
Know the atypical fracture: a patient on long-term bisphosphonates with prodromal thigh pain and a transverse subtrochanteric or diaphyseal fracture. Image the other femur too.

flow.title: Fall, then can't stand
flow.desc: Older adult after a low-energy fall; groin or hip pain, unable to weight-bear, leg often shortened and externally rotated.

flow.title: AP pelvis and lateral — then MRI if clean
flow.desc: Radiographs first; MRI for the patient who cannot bear weight despite normal films. Simultaneously work out why they fell.

flow.title: Block, not traction
flow.desc: Regional block and multimodal analgesia, fluids, review anticoagulants, ortho-geriatric co-management. Optimize in hours, not days.

flow.title: Fix or replace, within 24–48 hours
flow.desc: Fixation for nondisplaced neck and intertrochanteric patterns; arthroplasty for the displaced neck fracture in an older adult.

flow.title: Walk, and treat the bone
flow.desc: Mobilize day one, VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention, then osteoporosis therapy and a falls assessment before discharge.

redFlags: Cannot bear weight but the X-ray is normal — occult fracture. Get MRI; discharging as a soft-tissue strain risks displacement.
Subtrochanteric fracture with hemodynamic instability — the thigh conceals liters. Resuscitate and check for other injuries.
Any open wound over the fracture — antibiotics, tetanus and urgent debridement; this is no longer an elective-timing problem.
A fall with no adequate mechanism, especially with syncope, chest pain or new confusion — the fracture may be the least dangerous finding.
Prodromal thigh pain in a long-term bisphosphonate user — atypical femoral fracture. A transverse subtrochanteric break with a medial spike is the picture.
pearls: A hip fracture is osteoporosis until proven otherwise — and the majority of patients still leave without treatment for it. Being the person who starts it is genuinely high-value.

Zoledronic acid after hip fracture repair cut new clinical fractures from 13.9% to 8.6% (HORIZON-RFT, a 35% reduction) and all-cause mortality from 13.3% to 9.6%. The mortality figure came out of the safety analysis rather than a primary endpoint — quote it that way, because it is the part people ask about.

One-year mortality is about 15–30% — classically quoted as 20–30%, with contemporary series nearer one in five. Treat the diagnosis with the seriousness that number deserves, however routine the operation is.
The displaced femoral neck fracture is replaced rather than fixed because of anatomy, not surgeon preference — the retinacular blood supply is already torn.
Traction has no role. It persists by habit; the evidence does not support it.
The best predictor of walking again is how they walked before. Ask, and record it — it sets the goal for the whole admission.
impress: Present it as a geriatric syndrome with a fracture attached: 'low-energy mechanism, so this is a fragility fracture — I want to know why she fell, and she needs osteoporosis therapy before discharge.'
Name the classification and what follows from it: 'Garden IV, so displaced and intracapsular — the head's blood supply is likely gone, which is why we are replacing rather than fixing it.'
Ask for the block early. Requesting a fascia iliaca block in the emergency department reads as understanding that analgesia here is delirium prevention.
Quote the timing target and the reason: surgery within 24–48 hours, because delay tracks with pneumonia, delirium and pressure injury.
Close the loop nobody closes: 'who is starting the bisphosphonate, and who is doing the falls assessment?' That question is the difference between treating a fracture and treating a patient.

name: Low Back Pain
tagline: The most common musculoskeletal complaint in medicine — where the diagnosis is usually nonspecific, most of the skill is in excluding the few dangerous causes, and imaging early makes outcomes worse rather than better.
whatItIs: Pain between the lower rib margin and the gluteal folds. In roughly 85–90% no specific pathoanatomic cause is identifiable, and the honest label is nonspecific low back pain.
Timed by duration: acute under 4 weeks, subacute 4–12 weeks, chronic beyond 12. Most acute episodes improve substantially within about 6 weeks whatever is done.

Four buckets worth separating: mechanical/nonspecific; radicular (sciatica from disc herniation, usually L4–S1); spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication, eased by sitting or leaning forward); and serious/systemic — fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina, inflammatory disease, or referred pain from an aneurysm or viscus.

Degenerative findings on imaging are near-universal with age and correlate poorly with pain. Disc degeneration, bulges and facet arthrosis are common in people with no symptoms at all, which is why a scan often adds a label rather than an answer.
diagnosis: This is a red-flag screen first, not an imaging decision. Ask about bladder and bowel function, saddle sensation, progressive weakness, fever, weight loss, cancer history, steroid use, IV drug use, and trauma.
Characterize the pain: axial versus radiating below the knee, what eases it (flexion easing pain suggests stenosis), and whether it is worse at night or at rest.

Exam: gait, spine tenderness, straight-leg raise, and a focused neurologic exam. Roots overlap, so screen by movement rather than giving each root one job: L4 — knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion, patellar reflex, medial leg; L5 — great toe extension, dorsum of foot; S1 — plantarflexion, ankle reflex, lateral foot. Check perianal sensation and tone if cauda equina is a consideration.

Do not image nonspecific low back pain in the first 6 weeks without red flags. It does not improve outcomes and leads to more procedures. This is one of the most consistent recommendations in the field.

When you do image: MRI for suspected cauda equina, infection, malignancy or progressive deficit — urgently. Plain films for suspected compression fracture; ESR/CRP and blood cultures when infection is in play.

Consider axial spondyloarthritis in the young patient whose back pain is inflammatory: onset before 45, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, pain in the second half of the night, and improvement with exercise rather than rest.

meds.use: First-line pharmacotherapy for acute and chronic nonspecific pain
meds.note: First-line among the drugs, but non-drug treatment comes ahead of all of them; modest effect sizes, so use the lowest effective dose and check renal, GI and cardiovascular risk

meds.use: Short courses in acute pain with spasm
meds.note: Sedation and anticholinergic effects limit use, particularly in older adults

meds.use: Adjunct, and an option when NSAIDs are contraindicated
meds.note: The PACE trial found no benefit over placebo for acute low back pain — reasonable to try, but do not promise much

meds.use: Chronic low back pain, especially with comorbid depression
meds.note: One of the few medications with evidence in chronic rather than acute pain
Pregabalin did not reduce sciatica pain in a randomized trial and caused more adverse events

meds.use: Avoid; consider only briefly in severe acute pain when everything else has failed
meds.note: No better than non-opioids for chronic back pain in a randomized comparison, with more harm

meds.use: Not indicated for nonspecific low back pain
meds.note: Do not carry this across to malignant spinal cord compression, where dexamethasone is urgent. Cauda equina from a disc is a decompression, not a steroid

nursing: Screen for the emergency at every encounter: new urinary retention, fecal incontinence, saddle numbness, bilateral leg symptoms or progressive weakness. Escalate immediately — this does not wait for the morning.
Bed rest is not the treatment. Encourage staying active within comfort; prolonged rest slows recovery and deconditions.
Teach that hurting is not the same as harming. Fear of movement predicts chronic disability more reliably than the imaging does, and reassurance is an active intervention.
Assess function, not just a pain score — walking distance, sitting tolerance, sleep, work and mood. That is what treatment is actually aiming at.
Note the psychosocial 'yellow flags': catastrophizing, low mood, job dissatisfaction, ongoing litigation. They shape outcome and warrant a different plan.
For chronic pain, reinforce that exercise and self-management are first-line and that flares are expected rather than a sign of new damage.
medStudent: Lead with the red-flag screen, then say the words nonspecific low back pain when that is what it is. Naming it accurately is a clinical skill, not a failure to diagnose.

Cauda equina is the emergency. Urinary retention with overflow incontinence is the most reliable finding; saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica and reduced anal tone support it. Urgent MRI and surgical referral — do not wait for imaging to organize the referral.
Distinguish neurogenic from vascular claudication: neurogenic eases with flexion and sitting, is often worse walking downhill, and pulses are preserved.

For sciatica, know the trajectory: most improve without surgery. Discectomy relieves leg pain faster, but outcomes converge by one to two years — so surgery is for severity and progression, not for the MRI.

Non-pharmacologic care is first-line at every stage, not only in chronic pain: superficial heat, massage, acupuncture or spinal manipulation for acute and subacute pain, and exercise, multidisciplinary rehabilitation and psychological approaches when it becomes chronic. Say this before reaching for a drug.
Explain why early imaging harms: it finds age-appropriate degeneration, that finding gets treated, and the patient ends up with more procedures and no less pain.

flow.title: Back pain, and one question first
flow.desc: Axial or radiating pain; the first task is the red-flag screen, not a diagnosis or a scan.

flow.title: Dangerous, radicular, or nonspecific
flow.desc: Cauda equina, infection, malignancy and fracture get urgent workup. Radicular and nonspecific pain are managed clinically.

flow.title: Keep moving, treat the pain
flow.desc: Stay active, avoid bed rest, and explicit reassurance about the natural history. Non-drug options come first — superficial heat, massage, acupuncture or spinal manipulation — with NSAIDs, or a short course of a muscle relaxant, if drug treatment is wanted.

flow.title: At 4–6 weeks, not before
flow.desc: Most have improved. Persisting or progressive symptoms — or a new red flag — is what prompts imaging and referral.

flow.title: Exercise and function
flow.desc: Structured exercise, multidisciplinary rehabilitation and psychological approaches; consider duloxetine. Aim at function rather than a pain-free spine.

redFlags: Cauda equina syndrome — urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, reduced anal tone, progressive weakness. Emergency MRI and surgical decompression.
Spinal infection — fever, night pain, IV drug use, recent bacteremia, immunosuppression, or an indwelling line. Get MRI plus ESR/CRP and blood cultures before antibiotics if feasible.
Malignancy — known cancer, unexplained weight loss, pain worse at night or at rest, age over 50 with a new pattern. Cancer history is the single strongest red flag.
Vertebral compression fracture — osteoporosis, chronic steroids, or trauma, often with focal midline tenderness and pain on standing.
Ruptured or expanding abdominal aortic aneurysm — sudden tearing back pain, syncope, a pulsatile mass. Back pain that hurts this much this fast is not mechanical.
Progressive neurologic deficit — a worsening foot drop or spreading numbness needs imaging now, not at 6 weeks.
pearls: Most acute low back pain improves substantially within about 6 weeks whatever you do — improves, not necessarily resolves; a good number still have some pain at a year. That shapes the whole encounter: your job is to exclude danger, control pain and avoid harm.
Imaging early is a harm, not a neutral act. It finds degeneration everyone has, and that finding drives procedures without improving pain.
Urinary retention is the most reliable sign of cauda equina. A patient who is still passing urine normally has usually not developed it yet — but ask again, because it evolves.
Flexion helps stenosis — the shopping-cart sign. Extension makes it worse, which is the opposite of most mechanical pain.
Inflammatory back pain improves with movement and is worse with rest. That reversal in someone under 45 should raise axial spondyloarthritis rather than another course of NSAIDs and no follow-up.
M54.5 is no longer a valid code. Use M54.50, M54.51 (vertebrogenic) or M54.59 — a claim on the retired code gets rejected.
impress: Say the diagnosis honestly: 'this is nonspecific low back pain — no red flags, no indication for imaging today.' Confidence in that sentence is what expertise sounds like here.
Screen for cauda equina out loud, by name, including bladder function and saddle sensation. It shows you know which single diagnosis cannot be missed.
Explain the imaging decision as a benefit-harm judgment rather than a rule: early MRI finds degeneration everyone has, and that finding leads to procedures without less pain.
For sciatica, frame surgery correctly: 'discectomy gets the leg pain down faster, but by a year or two outcomes are similar — so we operate for severity and progression, not for the scan.'
In a young patient with morning stiffness that eases as they move, ask about it directly. Picking up axial spondyloarthritis in clinic is a genuinely impressive catch.
